breakfast.name: Brik (Fried Pastry with Egg)
ingredients: Malsouka (thin pastry sheets -- or spring roll wrappers)
instructions: Brik is the Tunisian filled fried pastry -- a Tunisian icon
Malsouka is the paper-thin Tunisian pastry -- almost translucent
The filling: tuna, capers, onion, harissa, parsley
An egg is cracked raw into the filling just before folding
The pastry is folded into a triangle and immediately fried
The goal: the egg white sets but the yolk remains runny
Eaten by biting a corner first so the yolk doesn't run out
Brik a l'oeuf is the Tunisian street food classic -- eaten in hand
breakfast.description: Tunisian fried pastry with runny egg -- malsouka (paper-thin pastry) filled with tuna, capers, onion, and harissa, an egg cracked raw inside, folded and immediately fried. The goal: white set, yolk runny. Bite a corner first. The Tunisian street food icon.

breakfast.name: Lablabi (Chickpea Soup)
ingredients: Stale bread (torn into pieces -- placed in the bowl)
instructions: Lablabi is the Tunisian chickpea soup -- the hearty street breakfast
Chickpeas in a simple garlic-cumin broth
Eaten by placing torn stale bread in the bowl first
The soup is poured over the bread -- the bread absorbs it
Customized at the table: harissa, olive oil, lemon, capers, tuna
A poached egg is often added on top
Eaten at lablabi street stalls in the morning
breakfast.description: Tunisian chickpea soup -- chickpeas in garlic-cumin broth poured over torn stale bread (the bread absorbs the soup). Customized at the table with harissa, olive oil, lemon, capers, and tuna. A poached egg on top. Eaten at dedicated lablabi stalls in the morning.

breakfast.name: Fricassee (Tunisian Fried Sandwich)
ingredients: Small brioche-like rolls (fried -- the bun itself is fried)
instructions: Fricassee is the Tunisian fried roll sandwich
The roll itself is fried -- a small brioche-like dough that is deep-fried
Split and filled with tuna, egg, olives, harissa, and potatoes
A compact, rich, complete street sandwich
The Tunisian fast food -- sold at every corner kiosk
breakfast.description: Tunisian fried roll sandwich -- a small brioche-like dough that is deep-fried as the bun, filled with tuna, hard-boiled egg, olives, harissa, capers, and boiled potato. The Tunisian street fast food. The fried bun is what makes it distinct.

breakfast.name: Chakchouka (Tunisian Shakshuka)
instructions: Chakchouka is the Tunisian origin of the dish known as shakshuka
The word chakchouka is Tunisian/Berber -- it spread to Israel with Tunisian Jewish immigrants
Peppers and tomatoes stewed together in spices
Eggs cracked directly into the stew and poached until just set
Eaten with bread for dipping
The harissa gives it the Tunisian heat and red color
Chakchouka pre-dates the Israeli-popularized version
breakfast.description: Tunisian spiced egg and tomato stew -- the origin of shakshuka. Peppers and tomatoes stewed in harissa, cumin, and coriander, eggs poached directly in the sauce until just set. The word chakchouka is Tunisian/Berber; it spread internationally through Tunisian Jewish immigrants to Israel.

lunch.name: Couscous Tunisien
ingredients: Couscous (semolina -- steamed twice in a couscoussier)
instructions: Tunisian couscous is distinct from Moroccan -- spicier and with more harissa
The couscous is steamed over the stew in a couscoussier (a two-part pot)
The steam from the stew flavors the couscous
Steamed twice: first once, then removed, rubbed with butter, then steamed again
The Tunisian version: more broth (the soup is a key part), and spicier than Moroccan
Harissa is stirred into the broth -- the red-orange color is characteristic
Traditionally eaten on Friday (the Muslim holy day) as the family meal
lunch.description: Tunisian spiced couscous -- semolina steamed twice over a spiced lamb and vegetable stew (in a couscoussier), the steam flavoring the couscous. Spicier and brothier than Moroccan couscous; harissa gives the characteristic red color. Friday family meal across Tunisia.

lunch.name: Tajine Tunisienne (Baked Egg Tart)
instructions: Tunisian tajine is completely different from the Moroccan slow-cooked stew
In Tunisia, tajine is a baked egg tart -- similar to a frittata or tortilla espanola
Made in a deep oven dish
The base: beaten eggs mixed with meat, herbs, cheese, and harissa
Baked until set -- it can be flipped or served from the dish
Served warm or cold -- travels well
The name confusion (Moroccan vs Tunisian tajine) is a common culinary mix-up
lunch.description: Tunisian baked egg tart -- completely different from Moroccan tajine (slow stew). Beaten eggs mixed with ground meat, cheese, parsley, and harissa, baked until set. Similar to a frittata. Served warm or cold. The Tunisian-Moroccan name collision is a common culinary confusion.

lunch.name: Kamounia (Lamb in Cumin Sauce)
ingredients: Lamb liver or beef (cut into pieces)
Cumin (a large amount -- this is the dominant spice)
instructions: Kamounia is the Tunisian liver or beef dish dominated by cumin
Kammoun = cumin in Arabic
The dish is essentially: meat slow-cooked in a sauce where cumin is the dominant flavor
A deeper, earthier Tunisian stew
Eaten with bread for dipping the sauce
lunch.description: Tunisian cumin-dominated meat stew -- lamb liver or beef slow-cooked in a sauce where cumin (kammoun) is the overwhelming flavor, with garlic, tomato paste, and harissa. Kammoun = cumin: the name describes the dish. Eaten with bread for dipping.

lunch.name: Merguez Sandwich
ingredients: Merguez sausages (spicy lamb sausages -- red from harissa and paprika)
instructions: Merguez is the Tunisian spicy lamb sausage -- now eaten across North Africa and France
Lamb and beef mixed with harissa, paprika, and spices -- the red color is characteristic
Grilled on a charcoal grill
Eaten in a baguette (the French colonial legacy in Tunisian food)
French colonization of Tunisia (1881-1956) left the baguette as the bread
Merguez + baguette + harissa: the Tunisian street sandwich
lunch.description: Tunisian spicy lamb sausage in a baguette -- merguez (lamb and beef with harissa and paprika, the red color characteristic) grilled over charcoal, eaten in a baguette with harissa and fries. French colonization (1881-1956) left the baguette as Tunisia's bread. Merguez has since traveled to France.

lunch.name: Mechouia Salad (Grilled Vegetable Salad)
instructions: Mechouia is the Tunisian grilled vegetable salad
The vegetables are grilled whole over a flame or under a grill until charred
Peeled and roughly chopped -- the char gives smokiness
Mixed with olive oil, cumin, and lemon
Topped with tuna, egg, olives, and capers -- the Tunisian garnish combination
Eaten as a starter or side dish
lunch.description: Tunisian grilled vegetable salad -- tomatoes, peppers, and onion grilled whole until charred, peeled and chopped, mixed with olive oil, cumin, and lemon. Topped with tuna, hard-boiled egg, olives, and capers. The char gives smokiness. Eaten as a starter or with bread.

dinner.name: Mloukhia (Jute Leaf Stew)
ingredients: Dried mulukhiyah leaves (jute mallow -- ground to a powder in Tunisia)
instructions: Tunisian mloukhia is very different from the Syrian/Egyptian mulukhiyah soup
In Tunisia, the dried leaves are powdered and used to make a very thick, almost black-green stew
The dish is slow-cooked for 2-3 hours until very dark and intensely flavored
The texture is thick, slightly gelatinous -- the dried leaf powder gives it body
This dish is particularly associated with Eid al-Adha
The deep, complex, almost bitter flavor is an acquired taste
Caraway is the Tunisian signature spice -- common in Tunisian cooking
dinner.description: Tunisian jute leaf stew -- dried mulukhiyah leaves ground to powder and slow-cooked with lamb for 2-3 hours until deep, thick, and almost black-green. Very different from the Egyptian/Syrian version (soup). Associated with Eid al-Adha. Caraway is the Tunisian signature spice. An intense, acquired taste.

dinner.name: Chorba Frik (Cracked Wheat Soup)
instructions: Chorba frik is the Tunisian green cracked wheat soup
Frik: dried green wheat (harvested before fully ripe and then smoked/dried)
The slightly smoky, nutty flavor of frik is what makes this soup distinctive
A classic Ramadan soup -- the first dish eaten to break the fast (iftar)
Eaten with lemon squeezed in -- the acid brightens the flavor
Shared across North Africa and the Levant
dinner.description: Tunisian green cracked wheat soup -- frik (cracked green wheat, slightly smoked from the early harvest process) simmered with lamb, tomatoes, and coriander. The smoky-nutty frik flavor is the soup's identity. Classic Ramadan iftar soup. Lemon squeezed in at the table.

dinner.name: Kefta (Spiced Meat Patties)
instructions: Kefta are the Tunisian spiced ground meat patties -- grilled
The meat is mixed with aromatic herbs and spices
Formed into patties or elongated shapes on skewers
Grilled over charcoal
Eaten with bread and mechouia salad
dinner.description: Tunisian grilled spiced meat patties -- ground lamb or beef mixed with cumin, paprika, harissa, onion, and parsley, shaped and grilled over charcoal. Eaten with bread and mechouia salad.

dinner.name: Ojja (Spiced Scrambled Eggs)
instructions: Ojja is the Tunisian spiced scrambled egg dish
A fragrant base: onion, peppers, tomatoes cooked in olive oil with harissa and spices
Merguez sausage added for protein and spice
Eggs scrambled in at the end
Similar to chakchouka but eggs are scrambled (not poached)
Eaten with bread
dinner.description: Tunisian spiced scrambled eggs -- merguez sausage cooked with tomatoes, peppers, harissa, and caraway, eggs scrambled in at the end. Similar to chakchouka but scrambled rather than poached. Eaten with bread for dipping.

dinner.name: Couscous Poisson (Fish Couscous)
ingredients: White fish (whole or large pieces: sea bass, grouper)
Chermoula (herb-spice paste: garlic, parsley, coriander, cumin, paprika, olive oil)
instructions: Coastal Tunisia has a fish couscous tradition -- the Mediterranean fish version
The fish is marinated in chermoula before cooking
Cooked in a fragrant tomato broth
The couscous is steamed over the fish broth
The coastal cities (Sfax, Sousse, Djerba) each have their version
Djerba island is particularly known for its fish couscous
dinner.description: Tunisian coastal fish couscous -- white fish marinated in chermoula (garlic, parsley, cumin, paprika), cooked in a harissa-tomato broth with vegetables, couscous steamed over the broth. The coastal tradition of Sfax, Sousse, and Djerba island. The Mediterranean face of Tunisian cuisine.

snacks.name: Harissa
instructions: Harissa is Tunisia's most important condiment -- used in almost everything
A paste of dried red chillies with caraway, coriander, and garlic
Caraway is the defining Tunisian spice in harissa -- most other harissas don't use it
Made at home in large quantities, preserved under olive oil in jars
Used in couscous, brik, chakchouka, mechouia, sandwiches
Tunisia is the world's largest producer of harissa by export
snacks.description: Tunisian chilli-caraway paste -- dried red chillies blended with garlic, caraway (the defining Tunisian spice), and coriander seeds. Used in everything. Made in large batches and preserved under olive oil. Tunisia is the world's largest harissa exporter. Caraway distinguishes Tunisian harissa from all others.

snacks.name: Makroudh (Date Semolina Pastry)
instructions: Makroudh are the Tunisian semolina pastries filled with date paste
A semolina dough made with butter and orange blossom water
Filled with date paste or almond paste, then formed into lozenges
Fried or baked, then soaked in honey or sugar syrup
The city of Kairouan (the holy city of Tunisia) is famous for its makroudh
Kairouan makroudh are considered the finest -- shipped across Tunisia and internationally
Often eaten at Eid
snacks.description: Tunisian date-filled semolina pastries -- orange-blossom-scented semolina dough shaped around date paste (or almond paste), fried or baked, soaked in honey syrup. The city of Kairouan is the makroudh capital; Kairouan makroudh are the most prized. Eaten at Eid.

snacks.name: Bambalouni (Tunisian Doughnuts)
instructions: Bambalouni are the Tunisian ring doughnuts
A simple yeast dough fried in hot oil
Ring-shaped -- stretched by hand into a ring before frying
Coated in sugar
Sold at coastal beachside stalls in summer
The Sidi Bou Said and La Marsa coastline is associated with bambalouni vendors
snacks.description: Tunisian ring doughnuts -- simple yeast dough stretched into rings and fried in hot oil, coated in sugar. Sold at beachside stalls along the La Marsa and Sidi Bou Said coast in summer. Simple, fresh, and beloved.

snacks.name: Asida (Sweet Semolina Porridge)
instructions: Asida is the Tunisian sweet semolina porridge -- eaten as breakfast or a snack
Coarse semolina cooked in water to a thick porridge
Served with a pool of olive oil and honey on top
The olive oil-honey combination is classic Tunisian
Eaten with a spoon, mixing the oil and honey into the warm porridge
snacks.description: Tunisian semolina porridge -- coarse semolina cooked to a thick porridge, served with a pool of olive oil and honey. The olive oil-honey combination is classic Tunisian. Simple and nourishing.

desserts.name: Assidat Zgougou (Pine Nut Pudding)
ingredients: Zgougou (Aleppo pine nut seeds -- ground to a paste: small black seeds from Pinus halepensis)
Nuts, rose water, pomegranate seeds (for garnish)
instructions: Assidat zgougou is one of Tunisia's most unique desserts
Made from zgougou: the small black seeds of the Aleppo pine (Pinus halepensis)
The seeds are ground to a dark paste -- intensely nutty and slightly resinous
Cooked with milk and sugar into a thick dark pudding
The color: very dark brown-black -- striking
Eaten specifically on the Prophet's birthday (Mawlid al-Nabi)
The zgougou seeds are harvested from the Tunisian pine forests -- a uniquely local ingredient
desserts.description: Tunisian pine seed pudding -- zgougou (ground Aleppo pine seeds: small black seeds from Pinus halepensis) cooked with milk and sugar into a thick, dark, intensely nutty pudding. The dark color is striking. Eaten specifically on Mawlid al-Nabi (the Prophet's birthday). A uniquely Tunisian ingredient.

desserts.name: Baklawa Tunisienne
instructions: Tunisian baklawa uses orange blossom water prominently -- the Tunisian flower-water signature
The Tunisian version is often smaller and denser than Turkish or Greek baklava
Sometimes made with malsouka (the Tunisian pastry) instead of filo
The nut filling: pistachios or almonds
The syrup: sugar with orange blossom water
desserts.description: Tunisian flower-water baklawa -- filo or malsouka pastry layered with butter and ground pistachios, baked golden, soaked in orange blossom water syrup. The orange blossom water is more prominent in the Tunisian version than in Turkish or Greek. Denser and smaller than Turkish baklava.

desserts.name: Tarte aux Amandes (Almond Tart)
ingredients: Almond cream filling (ground almonds, butter, egg, sugar)
instructions: The Tunisian almond tart reflects the French pastry influence during the protectorate (1881-1956)
A French-style tart shell with a Tunisian almond filling scented with orange blossom water
The French patisserie tradition was adopted and adapted
Tunisian patisseries (pastry shops) blend French technique with Tunisian aromatics
Orange blossom water is the Tunisian aromatics signature in sweets
desserts.description: Tunisian French-influenced almond tart -- buttery pastry shell filled with almond cream scented with orange blossom water. The French colonial patisserie tradition (1881-1956) left a permanent mark on Tunisian sweets, blended with Tunisian aromatics.

drinks.name: Teh bil Naana (Mint Tea)
ingredients: Fresh mint (spearmint -- a very large bunch)
Sugar (a large amount -- Tunisian tea is very sweet)
instructions: Tunisian mint tea is the social drink -- drunk multiple times a day
Green gunpowder tea brewed very strong
Enormous amounts of fresh spearmint added
Sweetened heavily with sugar
Poured from a height to create foam -- the technique and the froth are important
Served in small glasses
Offering tea is hospitality -- refusing is rude
The mint: always fresh spearmint, never dried
drinks.description: Tunisian mint tea -- strong green gunpowder tea with enormous amounts of fresh spearmint and heavy sugar. Poured from height to create foam. Served in small glasses. Offering tea is hospitality; refusing is rude. The froth and the pour height are important.

drinks.name: Citronade (Fresh Lemon Juice)
instructions: Citronade is the Tunisian fresh lemon drink -- a legacy of French colonial cafes
Fresh lemon squeezed and diluted to taste with water and sugar
The Tunisian lemon: very fragrant, thin-skinned
Served in cafes across Tunisia as the non-alcoholic refreshment
The French cafe culture: sidewalk cafes in Tunis and the coastal towns
drinks.description: Tunisian fresh lemon drink -- freshly squeezed Tunisian lemons diluted and sweetened, served in cafes. A legacy of French colonial cafe culture in Tunisia. The thin-skinned, fragrant Tunisian lemon makes the difference.

drinks.name: Boukha (Fig Brandy)
ingredients: Boukha (distilled from dried figs -- the Tunisian Jewish spirit)
instructions: Boukha is the Tunisian Jewish fig brandy
Distilled from fermented dried figs
Made by the Tunisian Jewish community (Jewish Tunisians: some of the oldest Jewish communities in Africa)
The Djerba island has had a Jewish community since at least the 6th century BCE
After Tunisian independence (1956) and especially after 1967, many Tunisian Jews emigrated to France and Israel
Boukha traveled with them -- now produced by the Bokobsa family in France
Clear and slightly sweet -- drunk neat or with mixer
Tunisia was 15-20% Jewish before 1956 -- now less than 2,000 remain
drinks.description: Tunisian Jewish fig brandy -- boukha, distilled from dried figs by the Tunisian Jewish community (one of Africa's oldest Jewish communities, on Djerba since the 6th century BCE). After independence (1956) and 1967, most emigrated to France and Israel, taking boukha with them. Now produced in France by the Bokobsa family.
